sentences.text: This meeting is being recorded.
Okay.
The white on my wife's side.
Yeah.
All very Irish.
Well, dad is Donegal now, mom is Dublin, I think.
Okay.
So yeah, Donegal's a wild place.
It is, it's great.
I love Donegal.
It's just, it's like there's no rules.
It's just completely outlaw country up there.
Yeah, it is.
You described, described her father well.
Oh really?
Yeah.
He was also Irish dancing champion.
English Irish dancing champion.
Okay, so she can do this with her legs.
Can you, can you keep up?
No, no, I can drink with the best of the Irish but do one.
Of the two things which is, which is a prerequisite kind of.
Yeah, yeah, exactly.
I get on with a dad, let's put it that way.
Yeah.
Good.
Andy, I got in touch.
I listened to one of your podcasts this morning actually with.
Is it Dom Hawes?
No, Dumb horse.
Yep.
Yeah.
I actually connected with him afterwards because his story is.
There's a lot of the pre stuff but his story and how he tried to do what he.
What he did is, is quite similar to the kind of challenge I took on.
So I'll give, I'll give you a kind of a quick synopsis of where I am financially qualified.
First of all, did NBA and university Liverpool stay.
Started a golf agency marketing agency, sold it to Wasserman in 17.
A bit hasty.
I kind of was in that for a long earn out and I, I didn't really, you know, I just was an entrepreneur.
Probably didn't even realize it because the company that I started was.
Was quite young.
Anyway broke that agreement went and joined another agency kind of as a founder or sort of a growth CEO.
Then Covid came I raise some equity for football league clubs.
Did a family business that nearly killed me.
And then the end of 23, started 24.
I looked at the football industry so the agency side of it.
So some big levers for change.
Very fragmented market, notoriously, you know, has a rep.
So my background would be more in the commercial sponsorship marketing side of it because that's, that's the agency in golf.
You have to make money on what you sell for them.
Football is a little bit different, different level of service that's applied to it.
I spent the last 14 months meeting agencies and agents to see what the opportunity was.
I didn't want to go down the road of going back in on the agent side.
I wanted to do something on.
On like an M A model.
Had a partner, have a partner who is experienced in that.
On the tech side.
He had just exited A business and the tech side, we looked at it, we said, okay, this could be interesting.
We met about 107 agents, agencies, lifestyle businesses, a lot of it.
Very hard to, you know, everything is adjusted ebitda.
No one really, you know, like no one runs the business for growth.
Very few.
So the challenge was always finding, you know, one agency that you could acquire as a platform and then kind of go from there.
So we had a backer in the US who had agreed terms with us and 2 million equity, assuming we can get super growth.

So assuming we could find businesses with historical EBITDA that we could raise debt on to kind of pay him back quickly and then he could maintain a share in the business to be able to win on the upside.
There's been a couple of big moves in the football industry.
150 million plus and the two of them over the last little bit of maybe four firms coming together.
So that's the model that we kind of started with.
And I don't want to run over the fact that it's 150, 160 million exit because they're sizable.
But that's what the opportunity in football.
The challenges in that we've always had was.
Investor money going in needs to understand the industry.
It's a very different agency model insofar as it's seasonal, it's based on transfer windows, it's based on, you know, sometimes there's a little bit of luck.
So you need to have a.
Your concentration of income is generally on one or two key assets in a 50 to 60 person stable.
We settled in one agency based in London, mid size, good agency, had an offer on the table of, you know, 10 million plus from one of the larger agencies to buy them.
They felt like they wanted to grow.
We had a deal struck before Christmas.
They also had a marketing department which I really liked.
So it's like athlete marketing, influencer marketing, which is, which is, which is what I was interested in.
The football side, it just turned out to be too problematic on the financials.
Their P L was pretty good.
Cash flow was terrible and the balance sheet was.
There was a fair, fair bit of shareholder deficit in it.
So we would have had to put a lot of money in and we couldn't convince investors to do it because their stable was too concentrated on a couple of key assets over the last little bit.
There's three shareholders.
One of the shareholders runs the commercial department and we've pivoted.
Whereas we were going to go football agency into marketing agency, now we're going to Flip it.
Because we have super access to the top 10% of athletes across golf, tennis and football and their agency is in Formula one.
They have some really good footballers.
I have really good access to some really good sports people in golf and tennis.
So we're flipping it and now we're looking at the M A strategy starting with digital sports marketing, athlete agencies and maybe eventually backing into the football side of it.
It's, it's better for us for a number of reasons, but we also think it's better for investor money.
But similar to Dom, I've built over the last 12 to 15 months two sides with not much money.
So you're doing, is you're building the, the pipeline and you're also building, you know, the investor side of it and it's kind of chicken and egg.
So we have a VC in Holland who's interested in it.
We have couple of private individuals in Germany that are in the sports industry and have exited recently that are interested in it but with nothing solid.

But we have very much pivoted away from let's buy a football agency because they're too expensive and there's too much risk attached to it for a first investment to let's get the marketing side of it set up.
We have four to five sports marketing agencies that are interested and kind of down the line a little bit over 50%.
One of them close to 100 that we could get a deal done and we can grow through that side of it and then we potentially back into the football agency if it was something that we wanted to do.
So that's where we are in it.
It's a pretty strong team.
Once I break it down of the individuals involved, a lot of experience, the main thing we're missing is someone who comes in and says listen, there's a checkbook, just go and get it done.
That's what we're missing.

But we feel like going the marketing route and marketing is like the wrong term to use but going the agency route that isn't transfers is the easiest way to get this business to a profitable state that we can then potentially leverage to be able to go, you know, to be able to use our own money or bank finance to be able to, you know, acquire into the football side of it.
Okay, so what are you looking for today?
How can I help you best?
Because obviously we are totally in this space and we've actually been working with a buy side client from the US which acquired an agency called OMM which we, we set up that deal.
So we're Kind of in the space and yeah, I mean there's several ways that we can help you.
But what is it that you need help with?
Obviously without a checkbook, but you're also stuck being able to attract a checkbook without having some deals on the table as well.
It is chicken and egg in that respect.
So I don't really like.
Listen, I probably shut off the email a little bit too quickly without doing the research on it.
I'm not 100% sure.
On the services that you guys offer, we are quite close on two smaller agencies and one further conversation in the next hour that could bring another one on.
So on the target side we're not too far away from that.
It would be good to understand what the services you guys offer, you know what they are, what the breadth of it is and then you know how, what's your experience?
It looks like you've a lot of more experience on the marketing side of it than we would, we would be more on the sports side of it.
On the football side of the golf.
Yeah, we are marketing.
So we're 100% marketing services.
Well 98% yeah.
But yeah, we've also worked on the buy side with sports stuff as well.
So kind of know both.
So let me just tell you we are then.
So we're, we're capital A, we're an M and A advisory for marketing services companies or buyers.
So we work on both sides.
Buy and sell side.
We have a marketplace for sellers agencies co and we have a buy side consultancy as well.
So we help our clients who are either high growth agencies who are looking to acquire or we also work with investors in a similar position as you are.
So we work from a stopped start as well.
And we also work with private equity or private debt helping them to find platform businesses and then bolt on.
So we work right across the board and all of the services are there.
I mean if you already sort of locating the targets yourself and closing those deals, then that's a big part of what we offer as well.
But if there was like piecemeal stuff that you wanted help with like due diligence or something like that, then I'm sure we, we could help.
But it's we, we are pretty much working end to end on deals with our clients.
So finding the targets, bringing them to the table, helping with negotiation and valuation, helping with due diligence and getting the door closed.
Okay, so from our like the way I just listening and, and like first impressions may be more of a.
Today like it sounds like it could be More of an evolved relationship insofar as like with the first one, we don't plan on just doing one.
You know, that's the starting point of this with the first one.
Considering the position that we're in where we have a lot of the work done.
The first one, I won't say easy enough but it should be straightforward enough to get it to a close because we know we've been there for the last eight months so we think we're going to.
And when I say agency, I mean if I'm being real, it's probably more of an acqui hire than it is an acquisition of an agency.
It's an individual with a couple of good clients more than an actual agency.
If it goes, you know, if it goes into conversations this afternoon with a bigger agency, 20 odd staff, you know, quite a, quite a, they're there for quite a number of years.

So there's legacy in it maybe that's probably a starting point for us to, to have a deeper conversation of we need some help and because someone's going to have to do the due diligence, we're not going to one be qualified or skilled enough to do it in that specific space and to know what to look for bar, you know, obviously a high overview but you guys do it on a daily basis and, and you know, we will be busy and doing other stuff as well and making sure investors are.

So there's possibly room in the, in, in the, the bigger one as a starting point potentially rather than, you know, the smaller one which obviously we'll be trying to, you know, get to close ourselves because we're quite close to that one.
Yeah, yeah.
So probably, it probably makes sense to carry on as you are and yeah, I don't, I don't think we would be able to, to offer you a huge amount of help anyway if you're already in negotiation.
But where we can help is once you've got that first one closed then I think being able to, to scale your search is probably where we'll provide the most value.

So what, what tends to happen is, you know, groups like the one that you're running will sort of hit a natural ceiling of being able to contact the low hanging fruit in their network, have those conversations and they, you know, the, the percentage of deals that close anyway is ridiculously small.
It's like less than 5% something stupid.
So you'll have a ton of conversations.
Like you said, 110 conversations.
Only a couple of those will end up getting close to closing or closing.
So what happens is people run out of steam quite quickly and that's when me and my team can come in and we can really scale up that outbound search and being able to bring on targets.
So we'll dig up people that you didn't even know existed, so we can outreach, you know, thousands and thousands of agencies in one go and then myself and my team will qualify those leads.
So we'll have initial conversations with them, make sure that they're available to do a transaction, that they're interested, they're not tire kicking.
Yeah.
And, and then bring them into your calendar and get those set up and then you have a conversation and if it's good, that we then help with that next stage.
So requesting information and you know, building towards an offer and due diligence.
So.
Okay.
Yeah, yeah.
Pretty, pretty clear then.
Pretty straightforward.

I think it's just like today is kind of discovery and say hello to each other and you know, as we, as we go from there, then let us, let us see can we get the first one across the line and if that minor miracle happens, there's probably lots of opportunity then from there on.
Yeah, I mean it is chicken and eggs.

I think that the main thing really is to, is, I mean, this is, you know, just advice from the off, but I'm sure you know what you're doing, but really it's a volume play because your expectation should be that nothing will get over the line.

Uh, so really at any given point you need sort of 10, 20 conversations to be happening or have or, you know, are about to happen because the, the, the worst position to be in is to have like an offer on the table and then somebody pushing back and trying to get the best.
And it's your only one for the deal.
Yeah.
And you've got nothing else.
So you're emotionally invested and they've kind of got you over a barrel because you don't, you don't have any more deals.
So.
So really what we're bringing is, is that sort of firepower so you're able to go into every sing without being emotionally invested, that you've got more deals in the pipeline.
And so you're just going from deal to deal, making sure that you put offers out on everything and so people can say no and then you just remove them from the process.
Sure, yeah.
How do you see the market at the moment from the buy side?
Is it active?
Yeah, hugely active.
I mean the majority of our deals and clients are in the US so it's a different market than the uk.
For sure.
But they are buying in the, in the UK as well and invest in the UK and Europe and it's.
Yeah, I mean it's up and down.
There's always a reason why it's.
It's down.
I find with most agency owners currently, Trump's a nut job.
So people are very wary about sort of spending money on marketing, it seems, but where, wherever the downs are, we tend to always.
There's always an opportunity for us.
Sure, there's opportunity there.
Yeah.
What about the sports side of, have you much experience on the sports side?
Yeah, so we, we did a huge amount on the, the sports side of things.
So what happened was we were working with a client, basically a team of investors in the US who were looking to buy into spatial computing.
Their background was cloud computing, spatial comp.
Like immersive, you know, mixed reality experiences.
So they're, they're really sort of cutting edge agencies that work in that space.
And we found a fantastic one in the UK that happened to be in the sports space and what do they call it?
Smart stadiums.
So it, that took us into that, that world then.
I mean, we, we, we also speak over the years to lots of different sports marketing agencies.
Actually sold one to Smile as well about three years ago.
I actually read your case study in that.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
So I mean, we're in and out of it, but the last six months we've been in it a lot because we're looking at stuff that now aligns with this OMM acquisition and more sporting stuff.
So.
So athletes, like money agencies involved in like specifically in.
More so focused on the athlete side or would, would.
Yeah, I mean we've not, we've not done a deal on either side of those, but we, we are always talking with those types of agencies as well, the talent types.
Okay.
Okay, very good.
Well, listen, I appreciate your time.
Yeah, no worries.
Nice to meet you.
You're doing something really exciting.
So one word for it.
Yeah.
Frustrating is probably the next word that comes to mind.
But if we can get this one done.
Listen, I come back and I'll see.
Can I.
Yeah, see, can we have a conversation with the next one, which I think is probably meatier and needs more help on.
Yeah, yeah.
And that's where you'll get the funding as well, I guess.
Once.
Yeah, exactly.
Yeah.
Because you really need to show like 2,2 million EBITDA to get the, the bigger investors really excited.
And what are you, what are.
Just if you could tell me, is it like anything from 4 to 10 or 11 times 12 times maybe at, you know, certain, certain acquisitions over a certain EBITDA.
Is it like in and around the 1 to 2 million?
You're probably talking what, 8 to 10?
Well, the.
So, I mean, there is no fixed multiples.
They're just averages really.
So if you're around the one two mark, you're probably somewhere between five, five and six and a half, five and seven.
But there's, there's various things that will take that up or down.
I mean, if it was an influencer agency, for instance, with a bit of tech involved, you could be all the way up at 14x.
So, okay, so tech is important then.

Tech definitely pushes up multiples for sure, because when we're looking for anything that's measurement related, then we're always looking very close to double figures as a minimum, even if they're relatively small businesses.
So, yeah, tech will certainly push up the multiples.
Yeah.
Okay, I've taken off your time.
Hopefully there's more on the next one.
I'll be in touch.
Yeah, I'll let you know.
Yeah, I look forward to it, Jamie.
Cheers, Andy.
Take care.
Have a great day.
Speak soon.
Cheers.

summary.overview: In the recent Business Development and Strategy Discussion meeting, Jamie Farrell shared his extensive background in golf agency marketing, highlighted his current focus on opportunities in the football industry, and discussed the potential pivot to digital sports marketing after a deal with a mid-size London agency fell through due to financial concerns. He is actively building a pipeline for both investor engagement and agency partnerships, having secured interest from a US backer and exploring leads in the Netherlands and Germany. Andy Day, representing Capital A, offered insights into the M&A landscape for marketing services, emphasizing the importance of having multiple deals in the pipeline and the potential for high valuations, particularly with tech involvement. The meeting concluded with actionable items for Jamie, including progressing a smaller agency deal independently and reaching out for assistance with larger deals as they develop, with an aim to demonstrate significant EBITDA to attract larger investors.
